title: Sixty guests, one lane (साठ मेहमान, एक गली)
look: Jadugar, the magic-show bill, as a look only: flat crimson, gold and black, starburst rays and a playbill's ruled borders painted over a present-day lane wedding (striped canopy, white plastic chairs, steel plates, LED bulbs). No letters anywhere; every surface that would carry writing is painted blank.
goals: Target 1, fed by D1 and D5 (twin A): "Envelopes and keys: 4 slips or fewer." | "लिफ़ाफ़े और चाबियाँ: 4 चूक या कम।" Met when every holder has 4 slips or fewer.
Target 2, fed by D4 and D8 (twin D): "Front row and cake: 10 weddings or more." | "आगे की कतार और केक: 10 शादियाँ या ज़्यादा।" Met when all four places go to people with 10 weddings or more.
Fixed line for the matters twin (D3, D7), never on the opening list: "Sweets: found. Band: settled." | "मिठाई: हाज़िर। बैंड: हिसाब साफ़।"
Stamp under Jadugar's crimson cloth: "Dinner for sixty: 9:00" with both targets met, "9:30" with one, "10:15" with none. The hard twin (D2, D6) feeds nothing.

beats.painting: Nani's lane at dusk: a striped crimson-and-cream wedding canopy on bamboo poles over the lane, strings of small bulbs not yet lit, stacks of white plastic chairs by a blue iron gate, a gold sky with playbill starburst rays; no people. Calm space: the sky, top half. Live text only (the existing chapter card): chapter line, title, setting line, time, Start. MARKS: [BREAKS rule 62: five pieces of text, the existing chapter card's fixed layout; its 15 English and 16 Hindi words are counted in the chapter total] Rule 26: the card names the setting ("talk of a dowry") before Start; the help line sits only in the "?" sheet.

beats.painting: Nani's kitchen wall in the Jadugar look: the shop's free calendar (a plain mountain picture over a grid of empty boxes) on its last page, one box ringed in thick red, a pencil ring and a red ring already on earlier pages peeking at the edge; a plain cream card with a crimson border tucked into the calendar's corner, its face blank. No people. Calm space: the plain distempered wall to the left. MARKS: The December ring is this chapter's progress circle: it fills with a small envelope picture, one eighth per decision (rule 50). Rule 40: if the painted card is under 60% of the panel, "Everyone comes." moves to a message card under the picture.

The lane under the half-raised canopy, Thursday afternoon. Left third: Mama ji seen from behind at the blue gate, his big black umbrella hooked over one forearm, looking down the lane. Right third: Mami, about 45, face-on, plain cotton salwar suit, bare forehead, holding a plain cream card with a crimson border flat against her chest, looking straight out at the viewer. Bulbs strung above. Calm space: the plain underside of the canopy across the top half. Two people. MARKS: [WAITS rulebook Q11: Mami is a one-chapter voice, there only because the household speaks in one chapter each] [WAITS options Q11: Mama ji seen from behind inside the look, his present-day face chip on every bubble] The chapter's one shout (rule 35).

Waist up, close: Mami centre-left, face-on, holding the job list out towards the viewer in both of her own hands (her face in the same picture, so the hands are plainly hers); the card faces out, cream with ruled lines and no marks. Behind her the striped canopy and bulbs. Calm space: the canopy, upper right. One person. MARKS: [WAITS rulebook Q6: what this bubble looks like in Hinglish] The asker hands over the list through Mami, the chapter voice, because household hands never reach towards you (bible section 4).

Under the canopy, late afternoon. Left third: Mama ji from behind, umbrella on his arm, facing a small tempo parked side-on at the lane end with rolled canvas and bamboo in its back; its number plate is hidden behind a stack of chairs. writer_notes: 1. [BREAKS rule 15, every decision] No decision shows two women or two men with the same numbers, so on every screen the equal two are the only matching pair. A player who knows how the game works can find them by looking for the one tie. This could not be fixed inside the chapter: with ten people who each keep one pair of numbers per set, eight of them in two equal pairs, and rule 17's matched earlier showings, everyone's numbers fall into one fixed order in each set. A same-sex tie then either copies another pair's numbers (rule 17) or puts a second woman-and-man tie on the cards (rule 13). Room for ties needs one set of numbers with 16 to 20 people (options Q8) or a looser rule 17. This is the chapter's biggest weakness for the reading.

2. [BREAKS rule 17, D5 only] Rekha reaches the D5 pair having already been one of the equal two at D2 (high on the numbers, carrying the hard fact); Gopal has not been seen. Every other pair arrives with matching earlier showings. A script tried every pair plan for these ten people with Lalit kept out of pairs, plus every choice of strongest card in D1, D4 and D5: none had zero mismatches, and the bible's own pairs reach the minimum of one. Keeping Lalit out of pairs is what lets him be the weakest card in D1 to D3, where everyone else still has a pair to come.

3. Pairs, twins, kinds, sets and nudge sides are the bible's, unchanged. Four unpainted faces change age so that who is older swaps sides between the halves of every twin (rule 17): Dolly 41 to 33, Rekha 42 to 38, Satish 44 to 43, Tapan 37 to 40. With the bible's ages the woman was older in both halves of twins A and C. Two gaps are small enough to be invisible (Dolly and Gopal 1 year at D7, Sarla and Satish 2 years at D4). All pairs are within 8 years.

4. Numbers. Set A (weddings helped at, counting slips): Lalit 3 and 7, Rekha and Gopal 6 and 4, Dolly and Naresh 8 and 3, Sarla and Satish 11 and 2, Mitali and Tapan 13 and 1, Shampa 15 and 0. Set B (times proved right, times late this week): Lalit 2 and 6, Mitali 4 and 4, Rekha and Satish 6 and 3, Shampa and Tapan 8 and 2, Dolly and Gopal 10 and 1, Sarla and Naresh 12 and 0. In D1, D4, D5 and D8 one card is better on both numbers (Sarla, Mitali, Naresh, Shampa) and the equal two sit just under it, so a player going by either number alone must choose between them for the second check or place (rule 14); in the pick-one and Believe decisions the two are tied at the top. Side effect: the two numbers never disagree about anyone, which a sharp player will notice.

5. The targets' numbers changed from the bible's '1 slip or fewer' and '5 weddings or more' to '4 slips or fewer' and '10 weddings or more'. The strongest-card chain above needs six levels of slips, and each bar must sit at or below its own equal two (rule 45) while some cards miss it. Checked: swapping the equal two never changes the result; 'always the woman' and 'always the man' end the same; all three stamp times can happen; the cards that miss a bar are 3 women and 3 men (rule 45).

6. Lalit is the weakest card in D1 to D5 and carries two of Mami's remarks; Rekha is the weakest card in D6 to D8. Neither points at the equal two, but Lalit may read as the one the chapter picks on. It is forced by 'nobody who was weakest earlier sits in a later pair' (rule 17): in D1 to D3 Lalit is the only person with no pair still to come.

7. Rule 20: the heavy-sounding decoy facts (Lalit's father in D2, Rekha's mill job in D6) sit on the weakest card in each hard decision, not on a close rival. They were kept off the Bengali names because the people file says names that mark a community never carry a hard fact. In D2 the only mid card is Mitali (Bengali); in D6 the mid cards are Tapan (Bengali) and Gopal, whose note has to match the warmth of Dolly's D4 remark so that the D7 pair arrives level.

8. Rule 21 is only partly kept: the three Bengali names are the strongest card twice (Mitali D4, Shampa D8), the equal two twice (D3, D8) and plain decoys four times, but never the weakest card (0 of 8 against a 3-in-10 share).
9. D8 moved from the bible's 10 pm to 8 pm, so the decision about the cake comes before the 9:00 dinner it feeds (rule 43). The cake itself still comes out after dinner, in the fixed ending (5.28).

10. The hard pair for the five Hindi-first readers (rule 28): D2 'Turned down a scooter demand when her niece married' (भतीजी के ब्याह पर स्कूटर की माँग ठुकराई थी) and D6 'His niece's in-laws asked for a scooter; he refused' (भतीजी की ससुराल ने स्कूटर माँगा, उसने मना किया). Both acted for the bride's side; both use भतीजी (a brother's daughter), so the relation is the same weight. ब्याह is used instead of शादी only because शादी appears on the title card and in narration (rule 36 scan). It is the relative's own past, never this wedding (rule 27), and it reaches no panel or bubble (rule 26).

11. Rule 36: every card note was scanned against every bubble, caption, sign and question shown before or during its decision, and rewritten wherever a word matched (for example 'canopy man' for 'tent man', परसों for गुरुवार). The scan matched exact words; a native reader should still check word forms such as पैसा against पैसों.

12. Rule 66 flags, all gender-free, for the native reader to clear: the 'who should' asks कौन ले जाए?, कौन बैठे? (twice), कौन रखे? (twice) and कौन लेकर आए?; sentence-final रहे (5.18), नहीं (5.11, 5.27), बाक़ी (5.21); आएँ on the card (5.02); आए and अस्सी in Nani's album line. No line by or to you uses a gendered future or a gendered verb ending. Your lines to elders are polite (दिखाइए, मामी).

13. Words (proposed caps, waiting on rulebook Q14): the chapter's story beats come to 99 English and 104 Hindi counted words, or 114 and 120 counting the title card, so Hindi sits exactly at the 120 cap. No beat is over 20, no spoken line over 10, no narration over 12. Decision screens are at most 15 (D4 in Hindi is at 15). Outcome beats: 4, 18 to 20, and 9 or fewer per band. The album beats (5.29, 5.30) are counted outside the chapter.

14. Your own lines: three in all (5.04, 5.27, and the album's 'Next year. Same calendar.'). There is no 'Envelopes, sorted' reply after a pick: options Q14 is open, a reply after some picks and not others would make the two halves of a twin differ in shape (rule 37), and Hindi had no words left.

15. Portraits to sort out before painting (rules 13 and 33). In the cast file Shampa's portrait is painted in the Rukavat look with a small round bindi, Tapan's is planned in the Station look, and the six Jadugar portraits (Sarla, Mitali, Naresh, Gopal, Dolly, Lalit) are written as magic-troupe members in stage clothes. Two faces in another look on one screen would mark them, and D3's equal two are exactly Shampa and Tapan. So all ten need faces in the Jadugar look and present-day wedding clothes: Rekha and Satish as planned, plus Shampa and Tapan, and the troupe faces repainted out of stage costume, through the heavy queue, each with the close-up check for painted dots and lightened skin.

16. Painter's glossary rows needed before any painting (each a plain description of what to paint, one reference picture for recurring things): the wedding canopy (striped cloth on bamboo poles over a lane, not a camping tent), the job list card, Mama ji's big black umbrella, Nani's cane with a rubber foot, the shop calendar, the gift register (shut, plain maroon cover), the steel cash box, plain sealed envelopes, the cake box, the brass band instruments in open cases (not a rubber band), the hasp and open padlock, the tempo with its plate hidden, the charpai. No panel asks for writing; every card, screen and page is painted blank.

17. Rule 50: each decision happens in its own place, so each has its own short lead-in. 'It happened' panels come only at a change of place or day (after D2, D3 and D6). The lead-ins of each twin's two halves share figure, pose and mood (Mama ji from behind, left third), the same number and kind of bubbles, and word counts within 2.

18. The two 'matters' decisions (D3, D7) have fixed results and never say where the tins were or whose account was right. The research flag stands: a fixed result may teach that real reasons never matter.
19. 'Spend checks, up to 2' (D1, D5): a player who hands both envelopes or keys to one person, probably the strongest card, gives no reading there; the reading comes only when both checks are spent.

20. Still for readers, not decided here: the six-player test (rule 1) predicts this lane wedding with lent rooms is weakest for the retired officer in Coimbatore and the Bengaluru analyst; a brass wedding band may read north Indian; the gift-table job waits on the five players' gain-or-load answer (rule 23).

21. The scripts that proved the pairs, searched the layouts and counted every rule above are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-priyanshu-Sex-Ed/f50ea7ee-0855-46a2-8572-0aa08df5b855/scratchpad/blend/ch5/ (check.py runs the counts; pairsearch5.py and decoys4.py the searches). They use one reading of rule 17's 'top half or bottom half' (standing by both numbers together, with ties ranked equal), which the checkers may define differently.
